result.proof:
**Given:** The open set $V$, its local $C^1$ graph-boundary property, the open neighborhood $U$, the map $\phi$, and the continuous function $f$ from the statement.

[F1] [[thm-graphs-of-continuous-functions-have-content-zero]]: the graph of a continuous function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^2$ has content zero in $\mathbb R^3$.

[F2] [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]: content zero means finite cube covers of arbitrarily small total volume; it passes to subsets and finite unions, and padding such covers with degenerate cubes makes the set null.

[F3] [[thm-jordan-boundary-criterion]]: a bounded subset of Euclidean space is Jordan measurable if and only if its boundary has content zero.

[F4] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded subsets of $\mathbb R^3$ are compact.

[F5] [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]: the continuous image of a compact space is compact, and a continuous real-valued function on a compact space is bounded.

[F6] [[thm-lebesgue-criterion-in-rn]]: a bounded function on a rectangle is Riemann integrable when its discontinuity set is null.

[F7] [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]]: the indicator of a Jordan measurable set is Riemann integrable and its integral equals its Jordan content.

[F8] [[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]]: the Riemann integral is linear, monotone, and bounded in absolute value by the integral of the absolute value.

[F9] [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]: a bounded function is integrated over a bounded Jordan set by extending it by zero to a containing rectangle.

[F10] [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]: a $C^1$ map with invertible derivative at a point has a $C^1$ local inverse near that point.

[F11] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: derivatives of composable totally differentiable Euclidean maps multiply in order.



**Given:** [F1]–[F11], the stated local graph condition, and the $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\phi$.

1.1 Put $S=\partial V$. It is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F4]. At each $p\in S$, the local graph condition gives rigid coordinates and an open planar set on which $S$ is the graph of a $C^1$ function. Choose a small closed nondegenerate rectangle inside that planar set so its graph lies within the boundary chart and covers a neighborhood of $p$ in $S$. Compactness gives finitely many such graph patches covering $S$. Each patch has content zero by [F1]. A rigid image of a cube of side $\ell$ lies in an axis-parallel cube of side $\sqrt3\ell$, so rigid coordinate changes enlarge the total covering volume by at most $3\sqrt3$. Thus each patch has content zero in the original coordinates. [F1, F4, algebra]

1.2 Parameterize a local graph patch at $p\in S$ by $\gamma(y)=(y,h(y))$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$; its derivative has rank two because its first two coordinates are $y$. Differentiate $\phi^{-1}\circ\phi=\mathrm{id}$ and use [F11] to see that $D\phi$ is invertible. Thus $D(\phi\circ\gamma)$ has rank two. Choose rigid target coordinates so the first two coordinates of this derivative are invertible. The inverse function theorem [F10] gives a local $C^1$ inverse for those two coordinates, so the third coordinate expresses $\phi(S)$ locally as a $C^1$ graph. The homeomorphism $\phi$ maps the local one-sided region $V$ to one side of that image graph. Hence $\phi(V)$ has locally $C^1$ graph boundary. [F10, F11, given]

2.1 By [F2], the finite union of the source graph patches in step 1.1 shows that $S$ has content zero. [step 1.1, F2]

2.2 The compact image $\phi(S)$ has a finite cover by the local graph patches from step 1.2. By [F1] each patch has content zero in its rigid coordinates, and the cube-cover comparison in step 1.1 transfers that property to the original coordinates. Therefore $\phi(S)$ has content zero. It is closed and bounded by compactness and [F4], so its boundary is a subset of that content-zero set and [F3] makes $\phi(S)$ Jordan measurable. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 The Jordan boundary criterion [F3] makes the bounded open set $V$ Jordan measurable by step 2.1. The closure $\overline V$ is closed and bounded, and $\partial\overline V\subseteq S$, so [F2]–[F4] make it compact Jordan. The compact image $\phi(\overline V)$ is bounded by [F5], and its boundary is contained in $\phi(S)$; [F2] and [F3] make it Jordan measurable. The open image $\phi(V)$ is bounded as a subset of $\phi(\overline V)$, and its boundary is $\phi(S)$; [F3] makes it Jordan measurable. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 The function $f$ is bounded by some $M\ge0$ on the compact set $\phi(\overline V)$ by [F5]. In a common containing rectangle, its zero extensions from $\phi(V)$ and $\phi(\overline V)$ differ only on $\phi(S)$, which has content zero by step 2.2. Their bounded difference $g$ has discontinuities only on that content-zero set, so [F6] makes it integrable. Moreover $|g|\le M1_{\phi(S)}$. By [F7], $\int 1_{\phi(S)}=\operatorname{cont}(\phi(S))=0$; monotonicity and the absolute-value estimate [F8] imply $|\int g|\le\int|g|\le M\int1_{\phi(S)}=0$. The zero-extension definition [F9] therefore gives equal integrals: $$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$ [F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, step 2.2] ∎



These are source ingredients adapted in the local proof, rather than an attribution of this complete lemma verbatim.

**Given:** Vectors $a,b,c\in\mathbb R^3$ with the standard Euclidean coordinates.

[F1] For $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ and $v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, $u\times v=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,u_3v_1-u_1v_3,u_1v_2-u_2v_1)$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).

[F2] $\langle u,v\rangle=u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).



1.1 Applying [F1] first to $b\times c$ and then to $a\times(b\times c)$ gives the three coordinates $\bigl(a_2(b_1c_2-b_2c_1)-a_3(b_3c_1-b_1c_3),\ a_3(b_2c_3-b_3c_2)-a_1(b_1c_2-b_2c_1),\ a_1(b_3c_1-b_1c_3)-a_2(b_2c_3-b_3c_2)\bigr).$ [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Expanding the first coordinate in step 1.1 gives $a_2b_1c_2-a_2b_2c_1-a_3b_3c_1+a_3b_1c_3=b_1(a_2c_2+a_3c_3)-c_1(a_2b_2+a_3b_3)$. Adding the zero term $b_1a_1c_1-c_1a_1b_1=0$ gives $b_1(a_1c_1+a_2c_2+a_3c_3)-c_1(a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3)$. Expanding the second coordinate gives $a_3b_2c_3-a_3b_3c_2-a_1b_1c_2+a_1b_2c_1=b_2(a_1c_1+a_3c_3)-c_2(a_1b_1+a_3b_3)$; adding $b_2a_2c_2-c_2a_2b_2=0$ gives $b_2(a_1c_1+a_2c_2+a_3c_3)-c_2(a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3)$. Expanding the third coordinate gives $a_1b_3c_1-a_1b_1c_3-a_2b_2c_3+a_2b_3c_2=b_3(a_1c_1+a_2c_2)-c_3(a_1b_1+a_2b_2)$; adding $b_3a_3c_3-c_3a_3b_3=0$ gives $b_3(a_1c_1+a_2c_2+a_3c_3)-c_3(a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3)$. By [F2] the three results are the coordinates of $b\langle a,c\rangle-c\langle a,b\rangle$. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A real number $s\ge0$.

[F1] For real $x$, $\sinh x=(e^x-e^{-x})/2$, $\cosh x=(e^x+e^{-x})/2$, $\tanh x=\sinh x/\cosh x$, and $\operatorname{sech}x=1/\cosh x$; $\cosh x>0$ ([[def-hyperbolic-functions]]).

[F2] $\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1$, $\tanh'(x)=\operatorname{sech}^2x$, $\tanh$ is strictly increasing, and $\tanh(0)=0$ ([[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]]).

[F3] If $a<b$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, some $c\in(a,b)$ satisfies $f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a)$ ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[F4] $e^{x+y}=e^xe^y$ for real $x,y$ ([[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]).

[F5] $e^x>0$ and $e^{-x}=1/e^x$ for real $x$ ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]).



1.1 Divide $\cosh^2s-\sinh^2s=1$ by $\cosh^2s>0$ to get $1-\operatorname{sech}^2s=\tanh^2s$. Let $f(s)=s-\tanh s$. Then $f(0)=0$ and $f'(s)=\tanh^2s\ge0$. If $s>0$, apply [F3] on $[0,s]$ to obtain $f(s)-f(0)=f'(c)s\ge0$ for some $c\in(0,s)$; at $s=0$ equality holds. Thus $s-\tanh s\ge0$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Let $g(s)=s^3/3-f(s)$. By step 1.1 and monotonicity in [F2], $s-\tanh s\ge0$ and $s+\tanh s\ge0$ for $s\ge0$. Hence $g(0)=0$ and $g'(s)=s^2-\tanh^2s=(s-\tanh s)(s+\tanh s)\ge0$. For $s>0$, [F3] on $[0,s]$ gives $g(s)-g(0)=g'(c)s\ge0$ for some $c\in(0,s)$; at $s=0$ equality holds. Therefore $s-\tanh s\le s^3/3$. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The definitions [F1] and reciprocal identity [F5] give $1-\tanh s=2e^{-s}/(e^s+e^{-s})$. Multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^s>0$ and using [F4] gives $1-\tanh s=2/(e^{2s}+1)$. This is nonnegative, and $e^{2s}+1\ge e^{2s}>0$, so $2/(e^{2s}+1)\le2e^{-2s}$. Together with step 1.1 this proves both claimed bounds. [given, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎



Hyperbolic functions and derivative identities: [[def-hyperbolic-functions]] and [[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]].

**Given:** The real-linear map $L$, its domain and codomain, and the stated $\operatorname{SO}(3)$ equivariance.

[A1] All products and transposes are ordinary real matrix operations. For $x,y\in\mathbb R^3$, $x^Ty=\sum_{i=1}^3x_i y_i$.

[F1] [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]: a nonempty closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^n$ is compact, and every continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb R^n$ attains its maximum and minimum. The supplier states this theorem in ZF.




1.1 Fix $D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ and define $q_D(x)=x^TDx$ on $S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x^Tx=1\}$. The sphere is nonempty, closed because $x\mapsto x^Tx$ is continuous, and bounded because each $|x_i|\le1$ there. The function $q_D$ is continuous because it is a finite sum of coordinate products. By [F1], $q_D$ has a maximum at some $e\in S^2$. [A1, F1, given, construct]

1.2 Let $X=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,d_2,d_3)$. The proper half-turns $Q_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1)$, $Q_2=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,-1)$, and $Q_3=\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1,1)$ each leave $X$ fixed. Equivariance gives $L(X)=Q_iL(X)Q_i^T$ for each $i$; because $L(X)$ is symmetric, these three equalities force every off-diagonal entry to vanish. [A1, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $y\in S^2$ satisfy $e^Ty=0$ and put $c(t)=(e+ty)/\sqrt{1+t^2}$. Then $c(t)^Tc(t)=1$ and differentiating at $0$ gives $c'(0)=y$. The differentiable function $t\mapsto q_D(c(t))$ has a maximum at $0$, so its derivative there is $0$: its right difference quotients are nonpositive and its left difference quotients are nonnegative. Differentiating gives $0=y^TDe+e^TDy=2y^TDe$, since $D^T=D$. By scaling, this holds for every $y\perp e$, so $De$ is a scalar multiple of $e$. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Let $E_{jj}$ be the diagonal matrix with a $1$ in position $(j,j)$ and $0$ elsewhere, and let the $j$th column of a matrix $M$ be the diagonal vector $(L(E_{jj})_{11},L(E_{jj})_{22},L(E_{jj})_{33})^T$. Linearity and step 1.2 give $\operatorname{diag}L(X)=M(d_1,d_2,d_3)^T$, where $\operatorname{diag}A=(A_{11},A_{22},A_{33})^T$. A permutation matrix $P$ permutes the coordinate basis; if $\det P=-1$, then $-P\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$ and $(-P)X(-P)^T=PXP^T$. Equivariance says $\operatorname{diag}L(PXP^T)=\operatorname{diag}(PL(X)P^T)$, hence $MPd=PMd$ for every vector $d$ and $MP=PM$. Equivalently $M_{ij}=M_{\pi(i)\pi(j)}$ for every permutation $\pi$, so its diagonal entries have a common value $c$ and its off-diagonal entries have a common value $d_0$. Thus $L(X)=(c-d_0)X+d_0(\operatorname{tr}X)I$. [A1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 If $z\perp e$, then $e^TDz=(De)^Tz=0$, so $e^\perp$ is invariant under $D$, and the restriction of $D$ to this two-dimensional plane is symmetric. Its unit circle is a nonempty closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^3$; repeating the argument of steps 1.1 and 2.1 on this invariant plane gives a unit eigenvector in $e^\perp$. The remaining one-dimensional orthogonal complement is invariant and consists of eigenvectors. Hence $D$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Only finitely many vectors are chosen in this construction; no arbitrary choice principle is used. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 By step 3.1 write an arbitrary $D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ as $D=OXO^T$ with $O$ orthogonal and $X$ diagonal. If $\det O=-1$, change the sign of one eigenvector; this changes $\det O$ to $1$ and leaves $OXO^T$ unchanged. We may therefore take $O\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Equivariance and step 2.2 yield $L(D)=(c-d_0)D+d_0(\operatorname{tr}D)I$. [A1, step 3.1, step 2.2, given, algebra]

5.1 Set $2\mu=c-d_0$ and $\lambda=d_0$. Conversely, for any real $\lambda,\mu$, the map $D\mapsto2\mu D+\lambda(\operatorname{tr}D)I$ is linear and equivariant: $QIQ^T=I$, and $\operatorname{tr}(QDQ^T)=\sum_{j,k=1}^3D_{jk}\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ij}Q_{ik}=\sum_{j=1}^3D_{jj}=\operatorname{tr}D$ because the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal. If two coefficient pairs give the same map, evaluation at $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,0)$ makes their $2\mu$ coefficients equal, and evaluation at $I$ then makes their $\lambda$ coefficients equal. This proves existence, converse, and uniqueness. [A1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎



The proof uses only proper rotations; the replacement $P\mapsto -P$ handles improper coordinate permutations specifically because the dimension is three. This classification supplies the linear isotropic form when those assumptions are imposed. It does not derive linearity, isotropy, objectivity, a fluid constitutive law, or empirical coefficient values.

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions stated in the formulation.

[F1] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function; the finite-torus Fourier-basis supplier assumes this principle.

[F2] [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]: normalized Haar measure on the unit torus is probability Lebesgue measure, and the product torus carries its product probability measure.

[F3] [[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]: Fourier coefficients use the normalized integral against the conjugate character, and finite character sums are trigonometric polynomials.

[F4] [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]: under Countable Choice, normalized torus characters form a complete orthonormal basis; synthesis and Parseval hold and the coefficient map is an isometry onto $\ell^2$ in the finite-subset-net sense.



**Given:** $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $N\ge1$, Countable Choice, and the normalized Fourier conventions in the Definition.

1.1 Under $x=2\pi y$, normalized measure on $\mathbb T^d$ pushes forward to $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$ on $Q_d$, while $e^{2\pi i k\cdot y}$ becomes $e^{ik\cdot x}$. Thus Fourier coefficients and the componentwise $L^2$ inner product are unchanged by this rescaling. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F4] to each of the $N$ components after this rescaling. The coefficient map identifies scalar $L^2(Q_d)$ isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d)$; summing the component identities gives the vector-valued coefficient isometry. The Countable Choice hypothesis is exactly [F1]. [given, F1, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Since $w_k^{2s}>0$, completion of finite symmetric coefficient arrays is the weighted $\ell^2$ space: truncating to $|k|_\infty\le M$ converges by convergence of the defining nonnegative series. Conjugate symmetry is preserved under these symmetric cutoffs and yields real representatives by uniqueness of Fourier synthesis. For $s\ge0$, $w_k^{2s}\ge1$, so the coefficient sequence is in $\ell^2$ and [F4] gives its unique $L^2$ representative. For $s<0$ this argument gives only the weighted coefficient completion and makes no $L^2$ claim. [given, F4, step 2.1] ∎

**Given:** The hypotheses stated in the formulation, including the explicitly adopted choice principle where indicated.

[F1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; full AC is adopted for the Sobolev completeness supplier used here.

[F2] [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]: $W^{1,2}$ consists of $L^2$ classes with first weak derivatives in $L^2$, with the sum-of-squares Sobolev norm.

[F3] [[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]]: under its stated full Axiom of Choice hypothesis, the stated $W^{1,2}$ space is complete.

[F4] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: the real $W^{1,2}$ pairing is bilinear, symmetric and positive definite.

[F5] [[def-hilbert-space]]: a real inner-product space is Hilbert when its induced norm is complete.



**Given:** Full AC, $d\ge2$, and nonempty bounded open $\Omega\subset(-R,R)^d$ with the weak-derivative convention in the Definition.

1.1 By [F2] and [F3], the real $W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ norm is complete under the stated AC assumption. Its closed linear subspace $H_0^1$, defined by norm closure, is therefore complete in the inherited inner product from [F4]. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 For each fixed $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ the functional $v\mapsto\int_\Omega v\cdot\nabla\phi$ is continuous in the $H^1$ norm, since its absolute value is at most $\|v\|_{L^2}\|\nabla\phi\|_{L^2}$. Its kernel is closed; the intersection of these kernels is exactly $V$. Thus $V$ is a closed real linear subspace of $H_0^1$ and is complete. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The inherited pairing is positive definite and complete on $V$, so [F5] makes $V$ a real Hilbert space. The only boundary condition used is the defining closure $H_0^1$; no converse density or arbitrary-domain trace theorem has been invoked. [given, F4, F5, step 2.1] ∎

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions stated in the formulation.

[A1] For each nonempty interval, an affine rescaling of $b(s)=\exp(-1/(1-s^2))$ for $|s|<1$, extended by zero, is a positive smooth compactly supported bump; its integral is positive and finite, so it can be normalized to one.

[A2] All integrations below are over finite intervals. Fubini applies to smooth compactly supported functions, and differentiation under these finite integrals is valid.



**Given:** A nonempty finite rectangle $\Omega$, the test-space seminorms in the Statement, and a zero-integral test $h$.

1.1 For each interval, choose an affine copy of the bump in [A1]. Every derivative on $|s|<1$ is the exponential times a finite sum of rational terms with poles of finite order at $|s|=1$; $e^{-1/(1-s^2)}$ tends to zero faster than every such power, so extension by zero is smooth. Its integral is finite and positive, so normalization gives $\theta_i$. For $d=1$, put $(Rh)(x)=\int_{a_1}^x h(s)\,ds$. Its derivative is $h$, and it vanishes near both endpoints because $h$ is compactly supported and has total integral zero. Its support is compact inside the interval, and its $j$th derivative is $h^{(j-1)}$ for $j\ge1$; the zeroth seminorm is bounded by $(b_1-a_1)\sup|h|$. [given, A1, A2, algebra]

2.1 For $d>1$, let $x'=(x_2,\ldots,x_d)$ and $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$. Then $\int H=0$ by [A2]. Assuming the construction in dimension $d-1$, define $$(Rh)_1=\int_{a_1}^{x_1}\bigl(h(s,x')-\theta_1(s)H(x')\bigr)\,ds,\qquad (Rh)_j=\theta_1(x_1)(R'H)_{j-1}(x')\quad(j\ge2).$$ Differentiating gives $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h-\theta_1H+\theta_1H=h$. The first component vanishes both before the support and after its total first-coordinate integral, which is zero; the other components are compactly supported by induction. [given, A1, A2, step 1.1, induction]

3.1 If inputs are supported in fixed compact $K$, each coordinate projection $K_i$ is compactly contained in $(a_i,b_i)$. Choose closed intervals $J_i\Subset(a_i,b_i)$ containing $K_i$ and the support of $\theta_i$; for the first component also include the interval hull of these supports. The recursive formulas then place every output component inside the fixed compact product $K'=\prod_iJ_i$. Every output derivative is a finite sum of fixed-bump derivatives times finite-coordinate integrals of derivatives of $h$ or its marginals. Such integrals have sup norm at most the interval length times the integrand sup norm, and differentiation in other coordinates commutes with integration. Induction therefore bounds each output seminorm by a constant times finitely many input seminorms. This proves fixed-support continuity. [given, A1, A2, step 2.1, induction] ∎

**Given:** The data in the Statement, with $x(0)=x_0\in\mathbb R^N$.

[F1] If $F$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in its state variable on an open domain, Picard–Lindelöf gives a unique local solution through every point of that domain ([[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]).

[F2] Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges to a real ([[thm-cauchy-criterion-via-lub]]).

[F3] If a continuous curve $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^N$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and $\|f'(t)\|_2\le M$, then $\|f(t)-f(s)\|_2\le M|t-s|$ for all $s,t\in[a,b]$ ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]]).

[F4] A continuous curve solves an IVP exactly when it satisfies the associated oriented Volterra integral equation ([[prop-first-order-ivp-is-equivalent-to-a-volterra-integral-equation]]).



**Proof technique:** direct polynomial bound and endpoint continuation.

1.1 Write each component as a finite sum $F_i(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in E_i}c_{i\alpha}x^\alpha$. On any bounded coordinate box, for each exponent $q\ge1$ the identity $a^q-b^q=(a-b)\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}a^{q-1-j}b^j$ bounds the difference of each monomial at two points by a finite constant times their Euclidean distance; telescoping over the $N$ factors and summing the finitely many monomials proves that $F$ is locally Lipschitz there. It is also continuous, so [F1] applies at every state. [given, algebra, F1]

2.1 Put $R_+=\max(1,R)$ and $M_R=\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^N(\sum_{\alpha\in E_i}|c_{i\alpha}|R_+^{|\alpha|})^2\bigr)^{1/2}$. Since $|x_j(t)|\le R$ for each coordinate, the finite polynomial sums give $\|F(x(t))\|_2\le M_R$ for all $t<T_*$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $0\le s<t<T_*$, apply [F3] to $x|_{[s,t]}$ to obtain $\|x(t)-x(s)\|_2\le M_R(t-s)$. Thus, for $t_n=T_*(1-1/n)$, $n\ge2$, each coordinate sequence $(x_i(t_n))_{n\ge2}$ is Cauchy because $|x_i(t_n)-x_i(t_m)|\le\|x(t_n)-x(t_m)\|_2\le M_R|t_n-t_m|$. By [F2], each coordinate has a real limit $\xi_i$; set $x_*=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose for each of the finitely many coordinates an index after which $|x_i(t_n)-\xi_i|<\varepsilon/\sqrt N$, and take the maximum of those indices. Then $\|x(t_n)-x_*\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^N|x_i(t_n)-\xi_i|^2<\varepsilon^2$, so $x(t_n)\to x_*$. For any $t<T_*$ and all sufficiently large $n$ with $t_n\ge t$, the same Lipschitz bound gives $\|x(t)-x_*\|_2\le M_R(t_n-t)+\|x(t_n)-x_*\|_2$; letting $n\to\infty$ yields $\|x(t)-x_*\|_2\le M_R(T_*-t)$, so $x(t)\to x_*$. The closed-ball bound passes to the limit, hence $\|x_*\|_2\le R$. [given, F2, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 By step 1.1 the polynomial field is locally Lipschitz near $x_*$. Apply [F1] to the IVP at $(T_*,x_*)$ to obtain a local solution $y$ on an open interval about $T_*$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, F1]

5.1 By [F4], $x(t)=x_0+\int_0^tF(x(s))\,ds$ for $t<T_*$ and $y(t)=x_*+\int_{T_*}^tF(y(s))\,ds$ near $T_*$. The limit in step 3.1 and continuity of $F$ extend the first identity to $t=T_*$. Define $\widetilde x=x$ before $T_*$ and $\widetilde x=y$ from $T_*$ onward, assigning the common value $x_*$ at $T_*$. The joined curve is continuous and the two integral identities add to its Volterra equation on $[0,T_*+\epsilon)$ for some $\epsilon>0$; [F4] therefore makes it a $C^1$ solution of the same ODE extending $x$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F4]

6.1 The extension in step 5.1 agrees with the original curve at every $t<T_*$ and is defined beyond $T_*$. This proves the statement. [step 5.1] ∎

1.1 Fix $V$ and $t_0\in I$. Its compact boundary is covered by finitely many relatively compact $C^1$ graph charts. On smaller compact chart pieces the graph functions have bounded derivative. Cover each two-dimensional base by squares of side $\delta$; the graph over each square has Euclidean diameter at most $C\delta$, hence lies in an axis-parallel cube of side $C'\delta$. There are $O(\delta^{-2})$ such squares, so the total cube volume is $O(\delta)$ and tends to zero. Thus for every positive bound the boundary has a finite axis-parallel box cover of smaller total volume, so $K=\overline V$ is compact Jordan in the sense of [L1]. The map $\chi_{t_0}$ is a diffeomorphism on a neighborhood of $K$, so $\chi_{t_0}(K)=\overline{P_{t_0}}$ and $\partial P_{t_0}=\chi_{t_0}(\partial V)$. Its derivative is bounded on finitely many compact chart neighborhoods of $\partial V$, so it is Lipschitz there. The image of each graph-covering square has diameter at most a constant times $\delta$, so it lies in an axis-parallel cube with volume $O(\delta^3)$; summing over $O(\delta^{-2})$ squares gives arbitrarily small finite cube covers of $\partial P_{t_0}$. Thus $\chi_{t_0}(K)$ is also compact Jordan. In particular, the volume integral over $P_{t_0}$ equals the corresponding integral over $\chi_{t_0}(K)$ for every continuous integrand because their difference is on the volume-null boundary. The fields are $C^1$ on neighborhoods of the swept closures. Pulling a common such neighborhood back by the continuous map $(t,a)\mapsto(t,\chi(t,a))$ gives an open set containing $\{t_0\}\times K$; compactness supplies an interval around $t_0$ and an open reference neighborhood $U_0$ of $K$ on whose product the fields are defined. Every sufficiently small open spatial ball $Q$ with compact closure in $\Omega_{t_0}$ is a material image $P_{t_0}$: its inverse image under $\chi_{t_0}$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain compactly contained in $B$. If a component of this continuous residual were positive or negative at an interior point, it would retain that strict sign on a small ball and have a nonzero integral, a contradiction. For $k\ne0$, differentiating the first equation and substituting the second gives $\ddot{\widehat z}+c_*^2|k|^2\widehat z=0$. With $\omega_k=c_*|k|$, its unique solution is $\widehat z(t,k)=\widehat z_0(k)\cos(\omega_kt)-i\rho_*(k\cdot\widehat v_0(k))\sin(\omega_kt)/\omega_k$, and integrating the second mode equation gives $\widehat v(t,k)=\widehat v_0(k)-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)k\int_0^t\widehat z(s,k)\,ds$. At $k=0$ both coefficients are constant. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Differentiation of these formulas recovers both mode equations and their initial coefficients. For each $k$, differentiating $E_k=|\widehat v|^2+(c_*^2/\rho_*^2)|\widehat z|^2$ gives zero: the two cross terms are $-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)[(k\widehat z)\cdot\overline{\widehat v}+(k\cdot\widehat v)\overline{\widehat z}]$, whose bracket is real, so its real part vanishes. Write $q=(z,v)$ and let $\mathcal L$ be the constant-coefficient first-order spatial operator in that system; recursively $\partial_t^nq=\mathcal L^nq$, which is a finite sum of spatial derivatives of order at most $n$.
